newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COFFEE--Colombia hears call for restructuring.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE--Colombia hears call for restructuring.

text.p: An influential banking and financial group has called for sweeping reforms of Colombia's troubled coffee industry to bring it back from what a top coffee official described this week as the "point of no return."

The reforms -- which would cut employment in the coffee sector dramatically -- are recommended in a report in the latest issue of Carta Financiera, a monthly magazine published by the National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF).

The report, entitled "Colombian Coffee and Survival of the Fittest," says there is a dire need to simultaneously cut production costs and boost productivity on every acre of land in the country's central coffee-growing region.

In 1995, an average of 25 60-kilo bags of coffee were produced on every hectare (2.4 acres) of coffee land in Costa Rica, the report says. It noted that this was nearly double Colombia's average output of 14 bags per hectare.

Colombia's production costs, meanwhile, averaged $0.94 per pound in 1995 while costs across Central America averaged no more than $0.70 per pound and were even lower in countries like Vietnam and Indonesia.
"In the medium-term, those producers who are unable to become more competitive will have to get out of the market," it said.

It did not explain how producers should go about bringing down production costs -- which have soared this year on the back of rising inflation -- but it hinted at the need for industrywide layoffs, saying 60 percent of the industry's costs stem from labor.
The report said Colombia's small and large-scale coffee growers were best placed to increase productivity and cut costs as part of a structural adjustment process.

Large growers, who represent just seven percent of all coffee farmers but control 43 percent of all plantations, have the economic resources and know-how to enact change, it said, adding that small growers were extremely "flexible in labor costs" since most of their farms were family-owned and operated.

According to ANIF, mid-sized growers -- who comprise 23 percent of Colombia's coffee farmers and occupy 34 percent of all plantations -- are the least efficient, and least likely to bring their production costs and productivity more into line with world standards.
"It's quite possible that the process of adjustment would convert any mid-sized producers who survive it into small or large-scale growers," the report said.

It did not elaborate, but the elimination of Colombia's medium-sized coffee farms could change the face of central provinces like Quindio, Risaralda and Caldas, where coffee has provided the middle-class with a way of life for generations and helped create a relative island of tranquility in a region that might otherwise be torn by leftist guerrilla activity.

Jorge Cardenas, head of the National Coffee Growers Federation, said this week that Colombia's coffee industry was "reaching the point of no return and of no longer being viable" because of a variety of factors that were conspiring against it.

Cardenas' main complaint, about the recent strengthening of the peso on rising oil revenues, was touched on in the ANIF, report which referred to the threat of so-called "Dutch Disease" and the country becoming overly dependent on oil.
ANIF put more emphasis on the need for deep-rooted change in the coffee industry than on calls for possible reforms of Colombia's exchange rate policy, however.

The peso's sharp rise since June has prompted widespread calls from exporters for a devaluation since it makes their products less competitive abroad and has cut sharply into their earnings in local currency.
A central bank official told Reuters Wednesday that the bank had no immediate plans to alter the peso's daily floating rate exchange band, however, and ruled out any swift devaluation.
